intro_en:
The Israel National Trail advances along the length of Nahal Raham amid spectacular and varied landscapes of granite, colourful sandstones and limestone rocks.

 Timna – Be'er Ora (53)
 Shehoret Canyon – Har Yehoram (55)
character_en: (For those walking north to south) A prolonged but not especially steep climb to a wonderful lookout from Mitzpe Amram, and a somewhat steep descent from there to the mouth of Shehoret Canyon.
pois_en: The Raham rock pools (Gevei Raham). Mitzpe Amram. Har Amir.
important_en: To get from Be'er Ora to the starting point, we walk about 2.5 km along a jeep track. In Be'er Ora it is possible to stock up on food at the minimarket.
The overnight campsite at the confluence of Nahal Raham and Nahal Atek lies beside the Israel National Trail, about 2 km from the starting point of the segment.

At the end point, the Nahal Shehoret overnight campsite is about 700 metres east of Shehoret Canyon and the end point of the segment. The campsite is accessible to any vehicle via a good road from the Arava Road.
The Israel Nature and Parks Authority usually brings a water trailer to the Shehoret campsite. It is advisable to confirm this with the Authority or in trail hikers' forums.
description_en:
In the community of Be'er Ora there is a minimarket as well as a trail hikers' campsite located outside the community. To get from it to the starting point of the segment, we walk along a jeep track for about 2.5 km heading north-west: we set out on a blue-marked road, then turn left onto a black-marked road that leads to the starting point of the segment.
From the starting point, the Israel National Trail continues on its way up Nahal Raham on a gentle climb.
We advance along the wide channel of Nahal Raham, which is between 300 and 400 metres wide. After we pass the confluence of Nahal Raham with its large tributary, Nahal Atek, the width of the channel drops to 100 to 200 metres. The large volume of runoff that Nahal Atek sends into the channel of Nahal Raham is evident in the widening of the channel.
At the confluence with Nahal Atek, at the junction with a blue-marked jeep track turning west, there is an unofficial overnight campsite.
We continue up Nahal Raham heading south-west. Several beautiful acacia trees are scattered along the channel, and we can enjoy a rest in the shade of one of them.
At the point where a black-marked trail heads off westward, another tributary flows into Nahal Raham, known as Nahal Shelalgon. It is so named because of the colourful rock outcrops of gypsum and clay rocks found up the gully.
At this point Nahal Raham turns south, and the Israel National Trail with it. On the rock walls on both sides of the channel, which gradually becomes narrower, grow bushes of the cartilage caper (Capparis cartilaginea), a shrub with large, light-green leaves. The cartilage caper grows in extreme desert conditions. In the Eilat area an average of 25 mm of rain falls a year, with great variability, between 0 and 40 mm a year. The average number of rainy days is just five. Despite the harsh habitat, the plant is green even in summer. Its thick leaves are protected by a waxy coating, a kind of very thin plastic layer covering the surface of the leaf. This is designed to reduce water loss from the surface of the leaves.
The cartilage caper also protects its leaves from being eaten by animals through three means: the plant is thorny, the leaves and other parts of the plant have a bitter, pungent taste, and a third and especially interesting means of defence: the caper recruits "guards" by secreting a sweet solution on its leaves and young fruits. Aggressive insects such as ants and wasps are attracted to the caper and keep the "sweet candy" for themselves alone. In this way they prevent other plant-eaters from harming the plant. When birds and small mammals are attracted to the fruit, they eat it and avoid chewing the seeds because of their bitter taste, and so the whole seeds are dispersed with their droppings.
We pass a trail junction located at the confluence of two streams. The Israel National Trail turns left with the black marking into the channel of Nahal Raham. A green-marked trail continues into the right-hand channel, Nahal Shani, another tributary of Nahal Raham, which rises on Har Shani near the border with Egypt. Nahal Shani cuts into red sandstone and forms the Red Canyon, from which its name is also derived: shani, meaning a dark red colour.
The Israel National Trail climbs on a prolonged but not steep ascent up Nahal Raham, until a section where large boulders lie in the channel. The trail passes between the rocks and climbs several rock steps. At the high step, we climb inside a chimney-shaped waterfall, with the help of iron rungs and handholds, up to the top of the fall.
We pass the "Raham Palms", several palm trees that grow in the channel of Nahal Raham and are rare in this area. After another half hour or so of walking, we reach the ridge line and the end of the climb. In relatively comfortable walking, the Israel National Trail climbs about 400 metres in total on this segment: from Nahal Raham in the Be'er Ora area, at an elevation of about 200 metres above sea level, to Mitzpe Amram at an elevation of about 600 metres.
On the ridge line, a red trail heads off left and north to Mitzpe Amram. It is highly recommended to leave the Israel National Trail and walk along the red trail for about 250 metres to the lookout, which offers a spectacular, colourful view including Har Amram, the Amram Valley, Har Amir, Har Shehoret, Har Shlomo, the Gulf of Eilat, the Arava and the Edom Mountains.
A beautiful description of the landscapes here was written by Azaria Alon, co-founder of the Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel, in his book "Trails in the Desert". Alon described the landscape of the Eilat Mountains and wrote that "the main part of the rainbow of colours is served up by the sandstone. But who says that only the sand creates colours? Here are the granites... the range of shades may be narrower, but every dark shade appears in them in a wild jumble."
From the ridge line we first descend via Ma'ale Amram to the saddle west of Har Amir. From the saddle and as the descent continues, we see the western flank of Har Amir. The mountain is built of sandstone in varied colours of pink, red and white. The forces of weathering have created and sculpted a multitude of shapes in the soft stone, producing enchanting sights of forms and colours; this special scenery accompanies the trail to the mouth of Shehoret Canyon, the end point of the segment.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel.
